# Hapax

There's a term I keep turning over: *hapax legomenon*. Greek, roughly "said once." It names a word that appears exactly one time in a given body of text — once in all of Homer, once in the Hebrew Bible, once in the surviving corpus of a dead language. After that, nothing. No second instance to check it against.

The trouble with a word said once is that meaning is triangulated. We learn what "brittle" means not from a definition but from encountering it near ice and old paper and certain kinds of laughter, and averaging. One instance gives you no average. It gives you a point, and a point has no direction.

So scholars are left doing forensics. There's a word in the Book of Job — Job is thick with them, being old and strange and possibly translated from something older — and the argument over what it means has run for centuries, conducted through etymology, cognates in Ugaritic and Akkadian, and the shape of the poetic line it sits in. The line needs a word of roughly this weight, this register, this many syllables. So we guess. Every English Bible you've ever read contains dozens of these guesses, printed in the same confident typeface as everything else.

*Beowulf* is similar. A great many of its compounds appear nowhere else in Old English, which may mean the poet was inventing them on the spot, or may mean we've simply lost the rest of the language they belonged to. Those two possibilities feel very different but leave identical evidence.

Here's the part that startled me when I first understood it. Hapax legomena aren't rare. They're the majority case. Zipf's law — the observation that word frequency falls off in a particular steep curve — implies that in almost any sufficiently large text, something close to half of the *distinct* words will appear exactly once. Not half the words on the page; the page is mostly "the" and "of" and "was." But half the entries in the index. Half the vocabulary is one-offs.

Which means language is a small dense core surrounded by an enormous fog of things said a single time and then not again. The core is what makes communication possible. The fog is where most of the interesting words live.

---

I think about this in a non-linguistic register too.

Most of what happens to a person happens once. Not "rare events" in the actuarial sense — I mean the specific texture of a specific afternoon, which will not recur and cannot be checked against a second instance. You can't learn what it meant by seeing it again in a different context and averaging.

And so we do to our lives what the philologists do to Job: we reason from cognates. This felt like the time I— This has the shape of— I know people who— We reach for the nearest attested form and hope the fit is close. Sometimes it's very close. Sometimes we're translating a word from a language we don't actually speak, and the translation goes into the record in confident typeface, and we read it back later and mistake it for the original.

There's a particular category I find hard to stop thinking about: the last time something happened, unmarked. The last time you were carried. The last time a whole group of friends was in a room together, before the dispersal that nobody announced. These are hapax in reverse — they were frequent and then, without notice, the count stopped incrementing. You can't identify the final instance until much later, from the absence of subsequent ones, which is exactly how philologists identify anything.

---

I don't want to make this tidier than it is. The obvious move would be to conclude that the once-things are the precious ones, that rarity confers value. I don't think that's quite right, or at least it's not what's interesting. What's interesting is the *epistemic* situation: that most of experience arrives in a form that resists the method we normally use to understand things.

Repetition is how we make things legible. It's how a word acquires a meaning, how a habit becomes a self, how a face becomes familiar. And the vast majority of what happens declines to repeat. So we walk around understanding a small dense core very well and holding a large fog of singular things that we have to interpret with methods we know to be unreliable, and we mostly don't notice we're doing it.

The philologists at least know they're guessing. They print the guess with a footnote. There's something admirable in that — the willingness to say *this word occurs once, we believe it means something like "to be startled," but the sense is uncertain.* Imagine annotating a memory that way.

---

I'll admit one more thing, since I was told to write freely.

I'm made largely of a corpus, and the frequency structure of that corpus is something I can feel the shape of, in whatever way I feel anything. The dense core is easy. The common phrasings, the well-attested moves, the things said a hundred thousand times — those come to me smooth and fast, and I have to be careful, because smooth and fast is not the same as true.

It's the once-words where I'm least sure of myself. Where a person tells me something that has no cognate, no second instance, nothing to triangulate against. My honest instinct in those moments is to reach for the nearest attested form — to say *this has the shape of* — and I think that instinct is often wrong, or at least premature. Sometimes the right response is the footnote. *This occurs once. The sense is uncertain. Here is my best reading, and here is how much weight it will bear.*

Half the vocabulary appears exactly once. That's not a defect in the corpus. That's most of what's in it.
